title: After an Apartment Fire: A First-72-Hours Checklist for Tenants
description: Displaced by an apartment fire? A step-by-step checklist for the first three days: shelter, insurance, your landlord, documents, receipts and your lease.
key_points: Do not go back inside a fire-damaged unit until the fire department says it is safe, and never restore utilities yourself.
Call your renters insurer quickly, ask what loss-of-use coverage pays for, and keep every receipt from day one.
Notify your landlord in writing and check your state's law and your lease before assuming you still owe rent on an unlivable unit.
body_html:
Apartment fires move fast, and the hours afterward can feel just as chaotic. Tenants often stand on the sidewalk with a phone, the clothes they are wearing and no clear idea what to do next. This checklist pulls together guidance from the U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) and other official sources into a practical order of operations for the first three days. It is general information, not legal advice; rules on leases and rent after a fire differ by state and sometimes by city.

Hour 0 to 12: Safety, shelter and the basics

  • Stay out until cleared. The USFA's After the Fire booklet says not to enter a damaged home or apartment unless the fire department says it is safe. Floors, ceilings and walls can be weaker than they look, and soot and runoff water can carry contaminants.
  • Leave utilities alone. Firefighters may shut off or disconnect gas, electricity or water before they leave. The USFA advises tenants not to turn them back on themselves.
  • Get emergency help with shelter. Local disaster relief groups such as the American Red Cross or the Salvation Army can help displaced residents find a place to stay, food, clothing and replacement medication. Fire departments and building managers can usually connect you.
  • Write down the details. Ask for the name of the fire department, a nonemergency phone number and the fire incident report number. Insurers and landlords commonly ask for the report later.
  • Find your pets. Frightened animals may bite or scratch; the USFA suggests leaving them with friends, family or a veterinarian while the unit is being cleaned.

Day 1: Insurance and money

  • Call your renters insurer right away. Ask what you should do first, whether the policy includes additional living expenses (often called "loss of use"), and whether you need approval before booking a hotel or hiring a cleaning or restoration company. The USFA recommends getting any cleaning estimate in writing and confirming who pays.
  • Know whose insurance covers what. According to the Insurance Information Institute, a landlord's policy generally covers the building itself, not a tenant's belongings or temporary living costs. Without your own policy, those losses usually fall on you.
  • Start a receipt folder. Keep every receipt for meals, lodging, clothing, toiletries, transportation and storage. The USFA notes that receipts may be needed by your insurer and to support losses claimed on your income taxes.
  • Report lost cards. Call your bank and credit card companies if wallets or cards were left behind.
  • No insurance? The USFA points to the Red Cross, religious organizations, community groups, public health departments and state or municipal emergency offices as possible sources of help.

Day 2: Your landlord and your lease

  • Notify the landlord in writing. Even if management already knows about the fire, send a short dated email or letter with your unit number, the date of the fire, how to reach you and a request for information on repairs and timelines. Keep a copy.
  • Ask direct questions. When will the unit be inspected? Will rent be paused or reduced while it is unlivable? Is another unit available? How will your security deposit be handled if you do not return?
  • Read the casualty or fire clause in your lease, then check your state's law. Some states have statutes on this. In New York, for example, Real Property Law section 227 lets a tenant surrender the premises and stop owing rent if the building becomes untenantable through no fault of the tenant, unless a written agreement says otherwise. Other states handle it differently, and local rent rules may add protections, so a legal aid office or tenant hotline can tell you what applies where you live.
  • Do not sign anything in a hurry. Be cautious about lease terminations, releases or new leases presented in the first days. Ask for time to review.

Day 3: Documents, inventory and next steps

  • Retrieve or replace key documents. The USFA lists items worth checking on, including driver's licenses, passports, Social Security cards, birth certificates, insurance policies, medical records and tax records. Each issuing agency has its own replacement process.
  • Handle burned cash carefully. The USFA advises touching damaged bills as little as possible and wrapping them in plastic. Mutilated currency can be submitted to the U.S. Treasury's Bureau of Engraving and Printing for possible replacement.
  • Build a loss inventory. When you are allowed back inside, photograph each room before moving anything. List damaged items with approximate age, cost and where they were bought. Bank and online shopping records help fill in gaps.
  • Secure the unit. If the apartment will sit empty, the USFA suggests telling local police the site will be vacant. Ask the landlord who is responsible for boarding up broken windows or doors.
  • Ask about taxes. The USFA recommends checking with an accountant or the IRS about tax provisions for people recovering from fire losses.

Look after yourself

Recovery from a fire takes weeks or months, not days. The USFA encourages people to rest and to ask for help rather than trying to do everything alone. If anyone in your household is struggling after the fire, disaster relief organizations can often point you to crisis counseling.

Quick-reference list

  1. Stay out until the fire department clears the unit.
  2. Get emergency shelter through the Red Cross or local relief services.
  3. Get the fire incident report number.
  4. Call your renters insurer and ask about loss-of-use coverage.
  5. Save every receipt.
  6. Notify your landlord in writing and keep a copy.
  7. Check your lease and your state's law on rent and termination after a fire.
  8. Replace documents and cards; photograph and list damaged belongings.

title: Renters Insurance After a Fire: Coverage, Loss of Use and Cost
description: What renters insurance pays after an apartment fire: belongings, liability and loss of use, plus replacement cost vs. cash value and typical premiums.
key_points: A landlord's insurance generally covers the building, not a tenant's belongings or the cost of living elsewhere after a fire.
Standard renters policies bundle three protections: personal property, liability and additional living expenses (loss of use).
NAIC data put the average renters premium at about $171 a year in 2022, with costs varying by state.
body_html:
When an apartment building burns, many tenants learn for the first time that the landlord's insurance does not protect them. According to the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I), a landlord's policy covers the building structure, not a renter's possessions or the extra expense of living somewhere else during repairs. That gap is what renters insurance is designed to fill. Here is how a typical policy works after a fire, and what to check before you ever need it.

The three parts of a standard policy

1. Personal property

This pays to repair or replace your belongings, such as furniture, clothing, electronics and kitchen items, when they are damaged by a covered event. Triple-I lists fire, smoke, lightning, vandalism, theft, explosion, windstorm and certain water damage among the perils commonly covered. Smoke and water damage matter after apartment fires: units that never saw flames can still be ruined by smoke or by the water used to fight a fire next door. Floods and earthquakes are generally excluded and require separate coverage.

2. Liability

Liability coverage responds if you are found responsible for injuring someone or damaging their property. In an apartment setting, that could include a fire that starts in your kitchen and damages neighbors' units. Triple-I says liability limits typically start around $100,000, and some experts suggest at least $300,000. Policies also commonly include a small amount of no-fault medical payments coverage for guests who are hurt in your home.

3. Additional living expenses, or "loss of use"

If a fire makes your apartment unlivable, this part of the policy helps pay for temporary housing. According to Triple-I, it pays the gap between what you usually spend to live and what displacement actually costs you. In practice, that means a hotel bill or short-term rental plus extra meal costs beyond what you would normally spend, not your entire budget. Policies set limits, sometimes as a dollar amount and sometimes as a time period, so check yours.

Replacement cost vs. actual cash value

This is one of the most important choices in a renters policy:

  • Actual cash value pays what an item was worth at the time of the loss, meaning replacement cost minus depreciation. A five-year-old couch may be worth very little on paper.
  • Replacement cost pays what it costs to buy a comparable new item, with no deduction for depreciation. Triple-I estimates this option costs about 10% more a year.

The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) cautions that a lower premium on an actual-cash-value policy can mean a larger out-of-pocket bill when you file a claim.

How much does renters insurance cost?

NAIC data cited by Triple-I show the average renters insurance premium was $171 in 2022, close to the $170 to $174 range of the previous few years. Costs vary widely by state. In 2022 Mississippi ($262), Louisiana ($243) and Oklahoma ($216) had the highest averages, while North Dakota ($123), South Dakota ($129) and Wyoming ($142) had the lowest. Your price depends on your location, coverage amount, deductible, claims history and discounts. The NAIC notes that insurers often give discounts for safety features such as smoke alarms and deadbolts, or for bundling with auto insurance.

Before a fire: set up your policy so it works

  • Make a home inventory. Walk through each room recording video or photos, including inside closets and drawers. Store it in the cloud, not just on a phone that could be lost in the fire.
  • Estimate your coverage amount honestly. The NAIC points out that even modest belongings add up to thousands of dollars once you price replacing clothing, electronics and appliances.
  • Check the loss-of-use limit. Compare it with what short-term housing actually costs in your area.
  • Know your deductible. A higher deductible lowers the premium but raises what you pay per claim.
  • Ask about high-value items. Jewelry, collectibles and some electronics may have sub-limits unless you schedule them separately.
  • Read the lease. Some landlords require renters insurance or a minimum liability limit. Whether they can is a matter of state and local law and your lease terms.

After a fire: filing the claim

  1. Call your insurer as soon as you are safe, and ask what you need to do first.
  2. Ask whether you need approval before booking temporary housing or hiring cleaners.
  3. Get the fire department incident report number.
  4. Photograph damage before moving or throwing anything away, unless it is a safety hazard.
  5. Keep every receipt for hotels, meals, clothing and transportation.
  6. Submit your inventory with the best available proof of value, such as receipts, bank statements or photos.
  7. Get adjuster decisions and settlement offers in writing.

If you believe a claim was handled unfairly, your state's insurance department accepts consumer complaints and can explain your rights under that state's insurance rules.

The bottom line

For roughly the cost of a streaming subscription or two a month (the NAIC puts typical policies at $15 to $30 monthly), renters insurance can cover belongings, liability and temporary housing after a fire. The time to confirm your limits is before the alarm goes off.

title: Apartment Fire Safety: Smoke Alarms, Escape Plans and Top Risks
description: NFPA and USFA data on why working smoke alarms matter, how to plan an apartment escape, and how to cut the biggest risks: cooking, space heaters and batteries.
key_points: NFPA found 59% of US home fire deaths in 2018-2022 happened where there were no smoke alarms or the alarms failed to work.
Cooking is the leading cause of home fires, and unattended cooking is the top contributing factor.
In apartment buildings, use the stairs, close doors behind you, and keep heaters and charging batteries away from exits and anything that burns.
body_html:
Apartment living puts many households under one roof, which means one person's fire can become everyone's emergency. The good news is that the most effective protections are simple and inexpensive. This guide draws on research from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) and safety guidance from the U.S. Fire Administration (USFA).

Smoke alarms: the single biggest difference

NFPA's 2024 report Smoke Alarms in US Home Fires, which analyzed fires from 2018 to 2022, found that nearly three out of five home fire deaths (59%) happened in properties with no smoke alarms (43%) or with alarms that failed to operate (16%). The death rate per 1,000 reported home fires was about 60% lower in homes with working smoke alarms. When alarms did not work, missing, dead or disconnected power sources were the most common reason.

The USFA's maintenance advice:

  • Test alarms monthly.
  • Replace batteries at least once a year in alarms that use replaceable 9-volt batteries.
  • Replace the entire alarm 10 years after its manufacture date.
  • Have alarms inside and outside each sleeping area and on every level.
  • Interconnected alarms, which all sound when one does, give earlier warning.

Renter tip: Many state and local laws require landlords to install smoke alarms, and some assign testing or battery duties to tenants. Requirements vary, so check your lease and local code. Texas, for example, requires landlords to provide smoke alarms and bars tenants from disabling them, according to the Texas Attorney General. Never remove a battery to stop nuisance alarms; ask management to fix or relocate the device.

Make an apartment escape plan

The USFA warns that you may have less than two minutes to get out once a smoke alarm sounds. A plan made in advance saves those seconds.

  • Know two ways out of every room where possible, and the location of every stairwell on your floor.
  • Pick a meeting spot outside the building.
  • Practice at least twice a year, including at night.
  • Use the stairs, never the elevator. USFA guidance for high-rises notes elevators may stop working or be taken over by firefighters.
  • Close doors behind you, including stairwell doors, and never prop fire doors open. Stairwell doors help keep smoke out of escape routes.
  • If you cannot get out, call 911, stay in a room with the door closed and seal gaps with wet towels.

Closed doors also protect you while you sleep. Research by the UL Fire Safety Research Institute, promoted under the "Close Before You Doze" campaign, recorded far lower temperatures and carbon monoxide levels in closed bedrooms than in open ones during test fires.

Risk 1: Cooking

Cooking is the leading cause of reported home fires and home fire injuries, according to NFPA. Its 2023 report found cooking caused an average of 158,400 reported home structure fires a year from 2017 to 2021, 44% of all reported home fires. Unattended cooking was the leading contributing factor. The USFA says unattended equipment was a factor in 37% of nonconfined residential cooking fires.

  • Stay in the kitchen while frying, boiling, grilling or broiling. If you leave, turn the burner off.
  • Keep a lid or baking sheet nearby to smother a pan fire, and turn off the heat. Never pour water on a grease fire.
  • Keep towels, packaging and oven mitts away from the stovetop.

Risk 2: Space heaters

USFA data show portable heaters account for only about 3% of home heating fires but 41% of fatal heating fires in residential buildings (2017-2019). Its rules of thumb:

  • Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heaters, radiators and other heat sources.
  • Turn space heaters off when you leave the room or go to bed.
  • Never use an oven to heat your apartment.
  • If your landlord is not providing adequate heat, report it in writing rather than relying on makeshift heating; many states and cities set minimum heat standards.

Risk 3: Lithium-ion batteries

E-bikes, e-scooters and other rechargeable devices have become a growing source of apartment fires. Fire officials advise buying devices and batteries certified by a recognized testing lab, using only the manufacturer's charger, charging on the floor away from your door and exits, and not charging while asleep or away. See our dedicated guide to lithium-ion battery fires for details.

A five-minute monthly checklist

  1. Press the test button on every smoke alarm.
  2. Check the manufacture date on the back of each alarm.
  3. Walk your escape route and make sure hallways and stairs are clear.
  4. Confirm the space heater is at least 3 feet from bedding and curtains.
  5. Look at chargers and batteries for swelling, heat or damage.

title: How to Get Your Security Deposit Back: A Renter's Guide
description: Document move-in and move-out, know your state's return deadline, and dispute unfair deductions. Examples from California, New York and Texas law.
key_points: Deadlines differ by state: for example, 21 days in California, 14 days in New York and 30 days in Texas.
Photos and a written condition checklist at move-in and move-out are your strongest evidence.
Landlords generally cannot charge for normal wear and tear, and several states impose penalties for bad-faith withholding.
body_html:
A security deposit is often the largest single sum a renter hands over, and getting it back can depend on paperwork you created a year or more earlier. Deposit rules are set by state law, and some cities add their own. The examples below show how rules differ; always check the law where your rental is located, or call a local legal aid office or tenant hotline.

How state deadlines compare

Every state sets its own rules for when and how a landlord must return a deposit. Three large states illustrate how much they vary:

  • California: The California courts' self-help guide says landlords have 21 days after move-out to return the full deposit or send an itemized statement of deductions with the balance. If deductions exceed $125, copies of invoices or receipts must be attached. Tenants can also request a pre-move-out inspection.
  • New York: Under General Obligations Law section 7-108, deposits are generally capped at one month's rent. Landlords must provide an itemized statement and return any remaining balance within 14 days after the tenant leaves, or forfeit the right to keep any of it. Tenants may request inspections before moving in and before moving out.
  • Texas: The Texas Attorney General says tenants must give the landlord a forwarding address to receive the deposit, and the landlord must return it, minus any deductions, within 30 days. Withholding requires an itemized list describing the damage.

Other states use different time frames, caps and interest requirements. Your state attorney general or housing agency usually publishes a tenant guide.

Step 1: Document everything at move-in

  • Take date-stamped photos and video of every room, including floors, walls, appliances, inside cabinets, windows, bathroom fixtures and any existing damage.
  • Fill out a move-in condition checklist, ask the landlord to sign it, and keep a copy. If your state offers a formal move-in inspection (New York does, for example), request one.
  • Email the photos to yourself or the landlord so there is a dated record.
  • Keep your lease, deposit receipt and any later repair requests in one folder.

Step 2: Understand wear and tear vs. damage

Landlords can typically deduct for unpaid rent and for damage beyond normal wear and tear, but not for ordinary aging of the unit. The Texas Attorney General gives a useful illustration: carpet that wears thin from a year of normal foot traffic is wear and tear, but carpet ruined by a leaking water bed is damage the tenant may be charged for. Faded paint, minor scuffs and loose door handles generally fall on the wear-and-tear side; holes in walls, broken fixtures and pet stains often do not.

Step 3: Move out the right way

  1. Give proper notice. Check your lease for required notice periods. The Texas Attorney General notes many leases require 30 days' notice as a condition of returning the deposit.
  2. Request a pre-move-out inspection if your state allows one, and fix what you reasonably can.
  3. Clean thoroughly and return the unit to the condition you received it in.
  4. Repeat your photo and video walkthrough after the unit is empty and clean.
  5. Return all keys and get a written acknowledgment.
  6. Give a forwarding address in writing. In some states, including Texas, this is required before the deadline starts to matter.

Step 4: If the deposit does not come back

  • Wait out the deadline, then send a written demand letter. Cite your move-out date, the state deadline, the amount owed and a date by which you expect payment. Attach your photos if you are disputing specific charges.
  • Challenge unsupported deductions. Ask for receipts or invoices; California, for instance, requires them for deductions over $125.
  • Know the penalties. In California, tenants can seek up to twice the deposit amount in additional damages if a landlord kept it in bad faith. In New York, a landlord who willfully violates the deposit rules can be liable for punitive damages of up to twice the deposit. Other states have their own penalty rules.
  • Use small claims court. Deposit disputes are a common small claims matter, and you generally do not need a lawyer. Check your state's dollar limit and filing deadline.
  • File a complaint. Many state attorneys general accept landlord-tenant complaints.

After a fire

If a fire forces you out and the lease ends, ask the landlord in writing how your deposit will be handled. Deposit laws still apply, but whether you owe rent, and for how long, depends on your lease and state law.

Quick checklist

  1. Photograph the unit at move-in and move-out.
  2. Keep a signed condition checklist.
  3. Look up your state's deadline and rules.
  4. Give written notice and a forwarding address.
  5. Send a demand letter if the deadline passes.
  6. Consider small claims court.

title: Landlord Repair Duties and the Warranty of Habitability
description: What the warranty of habitability means, how to request repairs in writing, and why withholding rent without following your state's rules can backfire.
key_points: Most states require landlords to keep rentals livable, but the details and tenant remedies vary widely by state.
Put every repair request in writing, date it, keep copies, and stay current on rent unless your state's law clearly allows otherwise.
Remedies such as repair-and-deduct or lease termination usually require strict notice steps, so check your state's procedure first.
body_html:
A leaking roof, a broken heater or a dead smoke alarm is more than an inconvenience; it can be a health and safety hazard. Most states recognize some version of a landlord's duty to keep rental housing livable, often called the warranty of habitability. But what that duty covers, and what a tenant may do when a landlord fails to act, depends heavily on state and local law. This guide explains the general framework and uses California, New York and Texas as examples. It is not legal advice.

What "habitable" usually means

In New York, Real Property Law section 235-b says every residential lease includes a promise that the unit and common areas are fit for human habitation and free of conditions dangerous to tenants' health or safety, and tenants cannot waive that protection. California recognizes an implied warranty of habitability through case law. A California Department of Real Estate guide lists basic standards such as working plumbing, gas, heat and electrical systems, a weatherproof roof and walls, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, safe exits, operable locks, and clean, sanitary conditions.

Texas takes a narrower, statute-based approach. According to the Texas Attorney General, tenants can demand repair of conditions that materially affect their physical health or safety, and landlords must supply smoke alarms and certain security devices such as keyed deadbolts and door viewers.

Across states, landlords generally are not responsible for damage caused by the tenant, household members or guests beyond normal wear and tear.

How to request repairs the right way

  1. Put it in writing. Even if you call or text first, follow up with a dated letter or email describing the problem, where it is, when it started and how it affects you.
  2. Use a trackable method if your state requires one. In Texas, for example, the Attorney General says tenants who want to use statutory remedies must send notice by certified mail with return receipt, registered mail or hand delivery, or else send a second notice.
  3. Keep copies of everything you send and receive.
  4. Document the condition with dated photos and video. Keep records of related costs, such as damaged belongings or medical visits.
  5. Allow a reasonable time. What counts as reasonable varies. Texas law presumes seven days, according to the state Attorney General; the California DRE guide says 30 days is usually considered reasonable, with shorter times for urgent problems like no heat in winter.
  6. Stay current on rent. In Texas, rent must be current when the landlord receives your notice for the statutory remedies to apply.
  7. Contact code enforcement if the landlord does not respond. City or county housing and health inspectors can cite violations and create an official record.

What not to do: withholding rent on your own

Stopping rent payments is the remedy tenants most often reach for, and the riskiest. Whether and how you can withhold rent depends on your state:

  • The Texas Attorney General warns that tenants do not have a right to withhold rent over repairs that do not materially affect health or safety, and that landlords may sue tenants who try. Texas instead provides specific remedies, discussed below, that require following the notice steps exactly.
  • In California, the DRE guide says withholding for serious defects can be permitted, but the landlord may still serve a three-day notice to pay or quit and file for eviction. It suggests setting withheld rent aside, for example in an escrow account, to show good faith.

Before you hold back any rent, talk to a legal aid office, tenant union or lawyer about your state's rules. A misstep can lead to an eviction filing, which can follow you for years.

Other remedies that may be available

  • Repair and deduct. Some states let tenants pay for repairs and subtract the cost from rent. In California, the DRE guide says the cost can be no more than one month's rent, the remedy can be used no more than twice in any 12-month period, and it applies only to serious health and safety defects after notice to the landlord. Texas allows a version of repair and deduct under its own conditions. Many states do not allow it at all.
  • Court orders. Texas justices of the peace can order landlords to make health and safety repairs costing up to $10,000, and tenants can go to justice court without a lawyer, according to the Attorney General.
  • Lease termination. Some states let tenants end the lease when serious conditions go unrepaired after proper notice.
  • Rent reduction or damages. Courts in some states can reduce rent for the period a unit was not habitable. New York's statute allows damages for breach of the warranty.

Protection from retaliation

Many states bar landlords from retaliating against tenants who request repairs or complain to inspectors, for example by raising rent, cutting services or starting an eviction. In Texas, the Attorney General says retaliation for a good-faith repair complaint is illegal for six months after the complaint. California law also prohibits retaliation for using repair remedies. Keep your written records; they are your proof of when you complained.

Fire-safety repairs deserve urgency

For a site focused on apartment fires, one category stands out: missing or broken smoke alarms, faulty wiring, blocked exits and inoperable fire doors. Report these in writing immediately, and call your local fire marshal or code enforcement office if they are not fixed promptly.

title: How to Spot a Rental Listing Scam Before You Pay
description: FTC data show renters lost about $65 million to rental scams since 2020. Learn the red flags, how to verify a listing and where to report fraud.
key_points: The FTC counted nearly 65,000 rental scam reports and about $65 million in losses from January 2020 through June 2025.
Demands for wire transfers, gift cards or crypto, pressure to pay before a tour, and below-market rent are classic warning signs.
Verify ownership through county property records and report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
body_html:
Searching for an apartment in a tight market can make anyone eager to lock in a good deal, and scammers count on that urgency. A December 2025 Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Data Spotlight found that people filed nearly 65,000 reports of rental scams from January 2020 through June 2025, with about $65 million in reported losses and a median loss of $1,000. Because most fraud goes unreported, the real numbers are likely higher.

Where rental scams start

According to the FTC, about half of people who reported a rental scam between July 2024 and June 2025 said it started with a fake ad on Facebook, and another 16% said it began with a fake Craigslist listing. Younger renters were hit hardest: the FTC found people in their 20s reported losing money to rental scams at roughly triple the rate of older adults, and the agency noted that some were targeted in Facebook groups students use to find sublets near campus.

Common scam tactics

The FTC describes several patterns:

  • Hijacked or fake listings. Scammers copy photos and details from real listings, or invent properties, then post them at attractive prices.
  • Money before a tour. They ask for an application fee, deposit or first month's rent before you have seen the unit in person.
  • Fake credit checks. They push you to "prove" your credit by following a link to a credit report site, which may sign you up for a paid membership with recurring fees.
  • Identity theft. They collect Social Security numbers, driver's licenses or pay stubs.
  • Self-guided tours. Some use access codes and lockboxes to make a fake listing seem legitimate.

Red flags

  • Payment by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency. The FTC says that anyone who insists on these methods is running a scam. These payments are very hard to reverse.
  • Rent far below the local market. A deal that seems too good to be true often is.
  • Pressure to decide immediately. The FTC's advice is to walk away from anyone who pushes you to commit quickly.
  • An "owner" who cannot meet you. Claims of being out of the country, on a mission trip or otherwise unavailable are common.
  • Requests for sensitive data too early. Until you have agreed to rent a place, the FTC says a landlord does not need your Social Security number or credit score.

How to verify a listing

  1. Search the address along with the owner's or company's name. The same property listed under different names or prices is a warning sign.
  2. Check the management company's official website to confirm the unit is actually listed there, and call the office using a number you find independently.
  3. Look up the owner of record in your city or county property tax or assessor database and compare it with the person you are dealing with.
  4. Ask agents for credentials and confirm they work for the company they claim. Many states let you look up real estate licenses online.
  5. Run a reverse image search on the listing photos to see whether they were copied from another site.
  6. See the unit in person, or have someone you trust do it, before signing anything or paying.
  7. Get the lease in writing and read it before paying.
  8. Pay safely. Use a method you can trace and dispute, such as a credit card or a check to a verified company, and get a receipt.

If you think you have been scammed

  • Contact your payment provider immediately (bank, card issuer, wire service or gift card company) and ask whether the transaction can be stopped or reversed.
  • Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The FTC also suggests reporting to local police, your state attorney general and the website that hosted the ad.
  • If you shared personal information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan and consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze.
  • Watch for follow-up scams, such as people offering to recover your lost money for a fee.

Displaced by a fire? Be extra careful

Tenants forced out by a fire often need housing quickly, which is exactly the pressure scammers exploit. Ask your insurer, landlord or a relief agency like the Red Cross about vetted temporary housing, and apply the same checks to any short-term rental.

title: E-Bike and Scooter Battery Fires in Apartments: Risks and Rules
description: Lithium-ion e-bike and scooter batteries cause deadly apartment fires. FDNY and CPSC data, certification rules and safe charging habits for renters.
key_points: FDNY reported 18 lithium-ion battery fire deaths in 2023 and six in 2024 after a push on safety messaging and enforcement.
CPSC says many lithium-ion battery home fires and deaths happen at night while batteries charge and families sleep.
Buy certified devices, use the manufacturer's charger, and never charge near your apartment door, in a bedroom or while asleep or away.
body_html:
Electric bikes and scooters are now a common sight in apartment hallways, and so are the risks that come with their lithium-ion batteries. When these batteries fail, they can ignite quickly and burn intensely, and an apartment fire that starts near the front door can block the only way out. Here is what the data show and how renters can lower the risk.

What the numbers show

New York City. The Fire Department of New York (FDNY) has tracked lithium-ion battery fires closely. It reported 268 such fires and 18 deaths in 2023. In 2024 the department counted 277 fires but six deaths, a 67% drop in fatalities that FDNY attributed to safety messaging, inspections, outreach and an advertising campaign. In a December 2025 year-end summary, the department reported one death from a lithium-ion battery fire in 2025 to that point.

Nationally. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) said in its report covering 2017 through 2024 that it was aware of 533 deaths connected to micromobility products overall, most involving crashes rather than fires. Of those, 19 e-bike deaths, 15 e-scooter deaths and 11 hoverboard deaths were tied to lithium-ion battery fires. CPSC notes its counts may rise as more death certificate data come in. The agency also warns that it has seen many lithium-ion battery home fires and deaths at night, while batteries were charging and families were asleep.

Why these batteries catch fire

Fire officials and CPSC point to several recurring factors:

  • Uncertified or low-quality products that have not been tested to safety standards.
  • Mismatched chargers. CPSC warns that "universal" chargers may fit a device but still be incompatible with its battery, which can cause a fire.
  • Modified or rebuilt batteries, including packs assembled from used or repurposed cells.
  • Physical damage from crashes, drops or water.

Charging is not the only danger. FDNY has said its 2023 data showed nearly 60% of lithium-ion battery fires involved batteries that were not being charged at the time.

Certification rules

New York City's Local Law 39 of 2023, which took effect September 16, 2023, requires e-bikes, e-scooters and their batteries sold, leased or rented in the city to be certified by an accredited testing laboratory. The city says e-bikes must meet UL 2849, e-scooters and similar devices UL 2272, and lithium-ion batteries UL 2271. The law covers sales and rentals, not devices already owned. Other cities and states have their own rules or none at all, so check before you buy. Wherever you live, a certification mark from a recognized lab is a sensible minimum.

Building rules: check your lease

Landlords and building managers may set their own rules on whether e-bikes and scooters can be stored or charged inside units, hallways or bike rooms. Those policies, and any limits on them, depend on your lease, local fire codes and state law. Read your lease and house rules, ask management for the policy in writing, and never store a device where it blocks a hallway, stairwell or exit.

Safe charging and storage habits

Drawing on FDNY and CPSC guidance:

  • Buy certified. Look for a mark from a nationally recognized testing lab such as UL.
  • Use the manufacturer's charger and battery. Avoid universal chargers and aftermarket batteries not approved for your device.
  • Stay present. CPSC advises not charging while sleeping or away from home, and unplugging when charging is done.
  • Charge in the right place. FDNY says not to charge near exits, including your apartment door, or in a bedroom.
  • Plug directly into a wall outlet, not an extension cord or power strip.
  • Charge on the floor and keep batteries at room temperature and out of direct sunlight.
  • Watch for warning signs. Stop using a battery that smells odd, changes shape or color, leaks or makes unusual noises.
  • Dispose properly. Never put lithium-ion batteries in household trash or recycling; take them to a battery recycler or hazardous waste site.

If a battery catches fire

Get everyone out, close the door behind you to slow the spread of smoke and fire, and call 911 from outside. Battery fires can reignite and release toxic smoke, so do not go back for belongings.

Bottom line

E-bikes and scooters are a lifeline for many renters who commute or work in delivery. A certified device, the right charger and careful charging habits go a long way toward keeping them from becoming the cause of the next building fire.
